kakekotoba.interaction: On the surface 'this year's autumn' is passing (秋も去ぬめり), but 飽き (weariness/growing tired of a lover) resonates beneath it — the poem is a complaint that the promised support (like dew that gives life to the mokuse grass) has faded, and the beloved has grown weary/indifferent, just as autumn departs. The double sense deepens the poem's reproachful tone toward a patron/lover who broke a promise.

Not a true kakekotoba but flagged for consideration; retained as single reading 'to depart/pass' — no second grammatically active meaning found, so not listed as a separate pivot beyond the あき pivot above.

jokotoba.text: 契りをきし させもが露を 命にて
jokotoba.function: The kami-no-ku sets up an extended metaphor: the speaker was promised support as vital as dew is to the sasame (mugwort/plant) — this elaborate image, longer than a single ku and specifically composed for this poem, leads into the emotional lament of the shimo-no-ku over the broken promise as the year's autumn departs.

honkadori.source_poem: なほ頼めしめぢが原のさせも草わが世の中にあらむかぎりは
honkadori.source_poet: attributed to a kami's oracle (cited in Senzaishū and various commentaries as an ancient god's utterance, sometimes associated with Kumano/Shimotsuke shrine legend)
honkadori.function: Mototoshi alludes to the legendary divine promise 'なほ頼めしめぢが原のさせも草' — a god's assurance that as long as the sasame-grass of Shimeji-ga-hara receives dew, one may trust in the promise. By invoking させもが露, Mototoshi accuses a patron (traditionally identified as the head of the Enryakuji, who had promised him a promotion) of breaking a promise as sacred as that divine oracle, now that the year's end (autumn) is passing without fulfillment.

kigo.note: 秋 (aki) explicitly marks the poem's temporal setting — the year's autumn is ending, which carries the classical connotation of things fading, promises going unfulfilled, and time running out, paralleling the withering of the sasame-grass without dew. It is the dominant seasonal image, anchoring the poem's mood of disappointment and impermanence as the year draws to its close.

bipartite.kami_theme: A remembered promise, likened to dew sustaining the sasame-grass, on which the speaker staked his very life/hope
bipartite.shimo_theme: The sorrowful realization that this year's autumn is passing without the promise being fulfilled
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku constructs an elaborate metaphor of dependency — trusting a promise as one trusts dew to keep grass alive — while the shimo-no-ku undercuts that trust with the plain, resigned observation that autumn (the deadline, implicitly) is ending. The pivot turns hope invested in a sacred-sounding vow into disillusioned lament, the passing of the season standing for the passing of any hope that the promise will be kept.
